strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear empirical evidence (Figure 1) that cross-attention VLMs substantially underperform on fine-grained visual understanding tasks compared to token insertion
Simple and elegant core contribution: allowing text tokens to self-attend within cross-attention layers, creating implicit gating without architectural changes
Comprehensive experimental validation across 9 diverse benchmarks with both training from scratch and adaptation of pretrained models, demonstrating broad applicability

Thorough ablation studies, particularly Table 8's demonstration that masking self-attention severely degrades performance, combined with attention visualization (Figure 7) supporting the implicit gating mechanism
Significant performance improvements over standard cross-attention (10-20+ points on fine-grained tasks) while maintaining inference efficiency benefits
Practical efficiency analysis showing 74% training memory reduction and demonstrated application to streaming video captioning with constant memory overhead
Modular design allowing efficient adaptation of pretrained insertion-based models with only 352M-680M new parameters
Strong commitment to reproducibility with promised code/model release and extensive experimental details
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contribution is a single modification to attention computation (Equation 2→3), appearing more as an engineering optimization than a fundamental advance in VLM design

Persistent performance gap to token insertion (~7% average, with gaps up to 13% on InfoVQA) without adequate investigation of why the fundamental gap remains, suggesting the core problem may not be fully addressed

Incomplete analysis of why text-to-text interaction specifically helps: the implicit gating explanation in Appendix A is somewhat hand-wavy, lacking rigorous justification for why self-attention creates effective gating

Training efficiency claims need qualification: Table 1 shows CASA training time (10h14m) is comparable to insertion (10h29m), and the comparison uses different model configurations (insertion reduced to 75% token limit), muddying practical advantages
CASA∨ variant shows 2-5% performance drops despite efficiency gains, limiting adoption when maximum efficiency is needed—insertion methods would be preferable in that scenario
Experimental setup concerns: insertion baselines use 75% of token limits and lower image resolution (672² vs 896²), making direct performance comparisons potentially confounded

Limited evaluation of streaming application: video captioning only compared to LiveCC (7B) baselines using a smaller 3B model; no comparison with other recent streaming approaches (e.g., StreamingVLM)
Missing ablations on hyperparameter sensitivity (local window size, number of CASA layers) and lack of analysis of what information flows through text-image vs. text-text attention
Implementation fragility suggested by footnote about FlashAttention-2 alignment constraints and potential edge cases with multiple images per window
No discussion of societal impacts, failure cases, or scenarios where CASA is inappropriate for deployment

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: Figure 1 effectively demonstrates the performance gap on fine-grained tasks (charts, documents) between cross-attention and token insertion approaches.

Comprehensive experimental validation: 9 image benchmarks, multiple architectural settings (from-scratch and adaptation), extensive ablations on design choices, and real-world streaming video application.
Practical modularity: CASA can be applied to pretrained models by training only added layers (~16-17% parameters), demonstrated with successful adaptation of Qwen2.5-VL.
Solid technical execution: Implementation details are clear, blockwise attention training is well-described, and ablations (Table 6-8) properly isolate component contributions.
Meaningful real-world application: Streaming video captioning demonstrates constant memory overhead versus insertion methods' linear growth, with practical latency benefits.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: The core contribution is straightforward—enabling text token self-attention within cross-attention layers. While effective, this is an incremental architectural modification without fundamental innovation.

Incomplete solution to stated problem: ~7% average performance gap to token insertion remains (Table 2). More critically, fine-grained tasks show 8-13% gaps (InfoVQA, ChartQA)—exactly the benchmarks that motivated the work, suggesting the approach doesn't fully address the core issue.

Shallow mechanistic analysis: The 'implicit gating' explanation via Figure 7 is intuitive but not rigorously analyzed. Why does text-to-text interaction specifically enable fine-grained reasoning? Table 8's -SELF ablation is expected (removing self-attention hurts), and the paper provides limited insight into the underlying mechanisms.

Efficiency gains are not novel: Table 11 reveals that ~4× memory reduction comes from not processing image tokens through FFNs—a benefit inherent to cross-attention, not specific to CASA's architectural modification. The added architectural contribution is incremental to the main efficiency gain.

Limited video evaluation rigor: LiveSports3K evaluation uses LLM-as-judge (GPT-4o) rather than reference-based metrics. Comparison to 7B LiveCC baselines versus 3B CASA conflates model size with architecture. Only one quantitative video benchmark; limited exploration of streaming-specific constraints.

Incomplete baseline coverage: Recent cross-attention improvements (e.g., StreamChat's FFN-based visual updates, register tokens) receive only brief discussion. More thorough comparison to existing cross-attention enhancements would strengthen claims.

Missing failure analysis: No discussion of failure cases, tasks where CASA underperforms, or systematic analysis of why fine-grained understanding remains hard despite text-to-text interaction. No exploration of window size sensitivity.

Implementation subtleties not fully addressed: Footnote 1 (page 4) reveals FlashAttention-2 causality constraints that may complicate reproduction. Hyperparameter choices (e.g., window placement) lack detailed justification.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly identifies and investigates why cross-attention VLMs underperform on fine-grained visual tasks (charts, documents, OCR)
Elegant and simple solution: enabling text self-attention in cross-attention layers is straightforward yet effective, facilitating adoption
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 9 benchmarks, multiple architectures, both training from scratch and adaptation scenarios, with solid baselines
Exceptionally thorough ablation studies: Table 8's masking experiments convincingly demonstrate self-attention importance; attention visualization provides interpretability
Strong practical demonstration: real-time streaming video captioning with constant memory cost while insertion-based methods OOM; comprehensive efficiency measurements
Technical soundness: proper use of Flash-Attention2, careful attention masking, detailed reproducibility specifications in appendix
Honest limitations discussion: acknowledges ~7% gap to insertion, discusses trade-offs between variants, no overclaiming
Clear presentation: well-structured paper with informative figures and comprehensive appendix; logical progression from motivation to validation
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core contribution is a straightforward modification (add text self-attention to cross-attention) rather than a novel architectural insight
Evaluation fairness concerns: insertion baseline trained at lower resolution (672² vs 896²) and shorter sequences due to memory constraints, weakening performance gap claims
Persistent performance gaps on motivated benchmarks: InfoVQA (-13.2 pts), ChartQA (-8.2 pts) gaps undermine the stated goal of closing the insertion-based performance gap
Limited streaming video evaluation: only LiveSports3K tested with modest win-rate improvements (39.0% vs 33.7% for compressed insertion); lacks diversity
Local attention window constraints under-explored: text can only attend within image-delimited windows, limiting long-range dependencies across images; no failure mode analysis
Generalization concerns: only 2B and 3B models tested; scalability to other model sizes, vision encoders, and architectures unclear
Architectural design choices poorly justified: three variants without clear guidance on which to adopt; CASA∨ placement (every 4th layer) appears arbitrary
Insufficient failure analysis: no qualitative error analysis on high-gap benchmarks (InfoVQA, ChartQA); why self-attention helps specifically on fine-grained tasks unexplored
Incomplete design space exploration: Table 5 shows FFN updates help (+2 pts) but dismissed for cost; suggests potential improvements not investigated
Implicit gating mechanism lacks theoretical justification: empirically demonstrated but without principled explanation for why softmax over text+image tokens provides better gating than prior methods

strengths: Systematic and well-motivated decomposition of five key design differences (D1-D5) between cross-attention and token insertion, providing clear insights into efficiency-performance trade-offs
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple settings (from-scratch training on Helium1-2B and adaptation of pretrained Qwen2.5-VL) with extensive benchmarking on 9 diverse VLM tasks

Strong practical demonstration of streaming video captioning benefits: CA maintains near-constant memory and latency while token insertion models exhaust memory resources, addressing a real application need
Valuable empirical finding that prior CA underperformance stemmed from training pipeline differences rather than fundamental architectural limitations, effectively reframing the design space

Solid experimental methodology with detailed ablations, efficiency measurements (throughput, memory, FPS), comparisons to recent SotA baselines, and good reproducibility (detailed appendices, promised code release)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the paper primarily revisits an existing mechanism (CA from Flamingo 2022) with straightforward variant combinations (CA^∅, CA^<, CA^{t+v}); no novel architectural contributions presented

Significant unexplained performance gaps on important fine-grained understanding tasks (ChartQA: 4.2%, InfographicVQA: 3.5% drops) without sufficient investigation of root causes or whether these limitations are fundamental or fixable

Insufficient analysis of visual history compression mechanism (D5): the streaming setup relies on gist tokens to preserve multi-frame information from single-frame windows, but why and when this works remains unclear; Table 4 shows non-trivial performance gaps (e.g., NExT-QA: 64.8→60.5) that deserve deeper investigation

Training cost comparison incompletely specified: paper reports tokens/sec throughput but absolute training memory usage not clearly compared; sequence length/batch size trade-offs for insertion models (halved/doubled) complicate fair comparison
Parameter-sharing variant (CA^∅) shows efficiency gains but unexplained performance degradation; lacks analysis of whether this trade-off could be addressed through alternative designs
Limited investigation of failure modes and error analysis for document/chart tasks; missing ablation testing whether CA with full visual history would recover performance

Gist token design appears somewhat ad-hoc (reusing post-image delimiters); lacks principled justification and ablation studies on design choices; unclear how much visual information is actually preserved
Video evaluation scope limited to sports videos (LiveSports3K); generalization to other video domains and comparison fairness (3B vs 7B models with LiveCC) not fully addressed

strengths: Systematic decomposition of five core design differences (D1-D5) between cross-attention and token insertion, providing useful conceptual framework for understanding efficiency-performance tradeoffs
Controlled experimental methodology with fair comparisons: training from scratch and adapting pretrained models under identical settings, properly adjusting batch sizes for token insertion baselines
Comprehensive benchmarking across 9 diverse tasks and multiple model sizes with reproducible controlled settings
Genuine practical validation: real-world streaming video captioning demonstrates near-constant memory and low latency where insertion-based models exceed memory limits (Figure 4)
Clear, well-organized presentation with effective visualizations of attention patterns and efficiency metrics
Addresses a real and timely efficiency bottleneck for long sequences and streaming video applications
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily an empirical validation that vanilla cross-attention with modern training performs better than previously reported; cross-attention itself is not new (Flamingo, 2022+)

Unresolved performance gaps on important benchmark tasks remain significant: ChartQA (75.9 vs 80.0, -4.1%), InfoVQA (51.8 vs 55.3, -3.5%) with no deeper investigation into whether gaps are fundamental to CA or addressable via improved training/architecture

Gist token mechanism (Section 3.2, D5) is under-engineered and under-justified: reuses implicit tokens from existing chat templates rather than explicit design; no ablation validating that gist tokens actually preserve visual memory; lacks comparison with explicit learnable memory tokens

Restrictive video evaluation setup uses single-frame windows for CA vs. multi-frame for baselines, limiting visual context; while gist tokens supposedly compensate, empirical evidence for this claim is indirect rather than direct

Missing mechanistic analysis: no attention pattern visualization, qualitative failure case analysis, or investigation of gist token representations; unclear whether performance gaps reflect fundamental CA limitations or training differences

Statistical rigor gaps: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing reported; for performance differences of 1-4%, significance matters; re-evaluated baselines use inconsistent evaluation protocols
Incomplete ablations on design choices: CA⊙ (parameter sharing) hurts performance without analysis of why; CAt+v shows marginal gains without clarity on when tradeoff is worthwhile

Streaming evaluation limitations: LiveCC uses LLM-as-judge (known limitations); quantitative gains modest (39.0% vs 43.2% for 7B baseline); wall-time improvements are convincing but evaluation metric itself is weak

Limited scope of applicability: practical benefits are primarily for streaming scenarios; contribution does not address when token insertion is necessary for multi-image reasoning tasks requiring richer visual history
Missing comparisons with complementary efficiency approaches: token compression is discussed (Table 5) but not thoroughly evaluated; no analysis of combining CA with compression techniques

strengths: Well-motivated research question addressing a genuine gap in understanding why cross-attention VLMs underperform despite favorable efficiency properties
Systematic and methodical analysis through D1-D5 framework that decomposes architectural differences between cross-attention and token insertion mechanisms
Rigorous experimental methodology with fair comparisons using identical training pipelines, addressing major weaknesses in prior CA work comparisons
Compelling practical demonstration of streaming video captioning where CA maintains near-constant memory (~6GB) and latency while token insertion models quickly OOM
Comprehensive benchmarking across diverse tasks (9+ benchmarks), multiple training settings, and thorough ablation studies on architecture variants and design choices
Excellent presentation with clear figures (especially Figure 2), honest reporting of performance gaps, and commitment to reproducibility through code/model release
Important finding that vanilla cross-attention is far more competitive with token insertion than previously reported when trained in identical settings
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the paper primarily compares existing mechanisms rather than proposing fundamentally new methods; variants (CA⊙, CA<, CAt+v) are straightforward modifications
Persistent performance gaps on fine-grained visual tasks remain unresolved: 4.1% drop on ChartQA, 3.5% on InfoVQA—these are non-trivial for applications requiring detailed visual reasoning

Incomplete investigation of D5 (multi-image history): the paper explicitly avoids exploring multiple past image tokens even in non-streaming scenarios, limiting understanding of the fundamental performance-efficiency trade-off

Shallow root-cause analysis: while D1-D5 identifies design differences, the paper lacks mechanistic insight into why specific tasks suffer more (e.g., why does lack of image history hurt ChartQA more than GQA?), with no attention pattern analysis or error case studies

Gist token approach for preserving visual history feels ad-hoc: lacks rigorous analysis of what semantic information is encoded, with no ablations on gist token quantity or design beyond exploiting chat template conventions

Video performance underexplored: consistent drops across all video tasks with only one dataset (LiveCC) tested for live captioning, and single-frame window design appears to be a workaround rather than principled solution
Generalization limitations: all experiments use Qwen's vision encoder, only tested up to 3B models, and compressed insertion baseline (most direct competitor) is underdeveloped
Training efficiency gains modest for adaptation scenario: Table 1 shows adaptation throughput is similar between CA and SA, with efficiency benefits primarily at inference rather than training
